item.title: ADHD & Neurodevelopmental Training
item.description:
ADHD & Neurodevelopmental Training Program

Train attention regulation, impulse control, and executive function — with or without medication.

Through neurofeedback, Interactive Metronome, and sensory integration, we strengthen the brain’s self-regulation capacity and aim for improved performance in daily life and academics.

Training Modalities

  • Neurofeedback: Real-time EEG feedback for self-regulation of target frequency bands
  • Interactive Metronome: Auditory timing training to improve attention, sequencing, and executive function
  • Sensory Integration: Balance, coordination, and sensory processing training

Target Population

  • Children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD
  • Those seeking non-pharmacological or combined training
  • Individuals needing improvement in attention, impulsivity, and executive function

All programs are individually designed based on prior assessment and consultation.

item.title: Biofeedback HRV

Biofeedback HRV (Heart Rate Variability)

Real-time monitoring of heart rate variability (HRV) to train autonomic nervous system balance, improving stress resilience and emotional regulation.

  4. Improves sympathetic-parasympathetic balance and stress recovery

Applications

  • Chronic stress and burnout
  • Performance anxiety and test anxiety
  • Emotional dysregulation
  • Holistic mind-body optimization

item.title: Comprehensive Attention Test (CAT)
item.description:
The CAT (Comprehensive Attention Test) is a standardized assessment that measures multiple sub-domains of attention in a multidimensional way, taking into account developmental characteristics and situational context across age groups. Beyond simply determining whether someone “focuses well or poorly,” it provides objective scores for selective attention, sustained attention, divided attention, working memory, and inhibitory control.

It is widely used to assess cognitive difficulties associated with ADHD, academic underperformance, impulse control problems, anxiety, and depression. The CAT can be administered across a broad age range — from children and adolescents to adults. It provides an attention profile with percentile ranks and standard scores based on age-group norms, and identifies specific strengths and weaknesses across sub-domains such as visual vs. auditory and selective vs. sustained attention. It also serves as a foundational data source for evaluating clinical difficulties such as ADHD, learning disabilities, impulse control disorders, and depressive/anxiety disorders, and for designing personalized interventions including cognitive training, neurofeedback, and psychotherapy.

Age Ranges and Subtests

The CAT uses different tasks suited to each age group. Game-format tasks are provided according to the developmental level of the examinee, with difficulty and stimulus type varying by age.

Early Childhood & Children (Ages 4 – Lower Elementary)

  • Visual Selective Attention: Quickly and accurately locating target stimuli among multiple images
  • Auditory Selective Attention: Distinguishing and responding to specific sounds
  • Sustained Attention: Maintaining consistent attention when the same stimulus is repeated
  • Working Memory & Inhibitory Control: Remembering previously presented rules and avoiding impulsive responses

Adolescents (Upper Elementary – High School)

  • Visual/Auditory Sustained Attention: Maintaining attention over extended periods
  • Divided Attention: Responding simultaneously to two types of stimuli (e.g., sound + image)
  • Shifting Attention: Flexibly shifting the focus of attention according to context
  • Working Memory: Retaining and applying rules and information over a set period of time

Adults

  • Complex Attention Tasks: Efficiently allocating attentional resources when visual and auditory stimuli are presented together
  • Sustained Attention: Maintaining concentration even in repetitive situations
  • Inhibitory Control Tasks: Suppressing unnecessary responses and selecting the target response
  • Cognitive Processing Speed: Response speed and accuracy related to focused attention

Assessment Overview

  • Duration: Approximately 40–60 minutes
  • Method: Computer-based visual and auditory stimulus tasks
  • Age Range: Ages 4 through adults

item.title: Computer-Based Training (CBT)
item.description:
What is Computer-Based Training (CBT)?

Computer-Based Training (CBT) is a program that systematically trains specific cognitive abilities — including attention, memory, executive function, and processing speed — using digital devices such as computers, tablets, and smartphones.

Just as physical exercise improves fitness through repeated use of the body, CBT is grounded in the theory of neuroplasticity: the idea that cognitive abilities can be maintained or improved through deliberate and structured use of the brain.

At ConnectedMind Cognitive Science Institute, we use CBT programs and visual-perceptual training tools to deliver individually tailored cognitive training.

Training Principles

  1. Difficulty automatically adjusts to the individual’s cognitive level
  2. Trains multiple cognitive domains: attention, working memory, processing speed, executive function
  3. Performance is quantitatively recorded to track training progress
  4. Structured protocol for systematic cognitive rehabilitation

Applications

  • ADHD and learning difficulties
  • Cognitive function decline
  • Need for improved processing speed and working memory
  • Children and adults seeking focused attention training

item.title: ConnectedMind Cognitive Profiling
item.description:
What is ConnectedMind Cognitive Profiling?

ConnectedMind Cognitive Profiling is not simply a test to determine whether there is a “problem” or not. It is a process of comprehensively understanding a person’s cognitive strengths and vulnerabilities, emotional state, and neurophysiological patterns to design an optimized training plan for the individual.

From developmental challenges in children and adolescents to burnout, sleep problems, social anxiety, and reduced focus in adults — regardless of age, we help you deeply understand who you are today and explore the path forward together.

Assessment Areas

Cognitive & Executive Function

  • Intelligence Test (K-WISC-V / K-WAIS): memory, problem-solving, processing speed
  • CAT Comprehensive Attention Test: selective, sustained, and divided attention; inhibitory control
  • Stroop Test, Trail Making Test: executive function, cognitive flexibility

Neurophysiological Evaluation

  • QEEG Brain Function Assessment: brainwave pattern analysis, target frequency setting for training

Emotion & Personality

  • MMPI-2 (adults) / MMPI-A (adolescents): personality and mental health assessment
  • Temperament and Character Inventory (TCI): dispositional characteristics
  • Anxiety & Depression Scales: emotional dysregulation assessment

Children & Adolescents — Additional Areas

  • Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL, K-BASC)
  • Learning style assessment, reading assessment
  • Parent interview and school adjustment evaluation

Assessment Process

  • Duration: 2–3 hours (may be split into 2 sessions if needed)
  • Target: Children aged 5 and above through adults
  • Method: 1:1 individual assessment with a specialist, questionnaires, interview
  • Report: Comprehensive interpretive report and feedback consultation within 1–2 weeks after completion

Recommended For

Children & Adolescents

  • When attention problems, impulse control issues, or academic underperformance are a concern
  • When emotional difficulties such as anxiety, depression, or anger are recurring
  • When you want an objective assessment of developmental strengths and potential
  • When school life or peer relationships are difficult

Adults

  • When chronic fatigue or burnout is affecting daily performance
  • When sleep problems or arousal regulation difficulties persist
  • When social anxiety, emotional dysregulation, or relationship exhaustion is ongoing
  • When reduced focus or memory decline is a concern
  • When you want an objective understanding of your cognitive and emotional profile

item.title: Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment
item.description:
What is the Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment?

The Eye Movement Based Reading Assessment uses eye-tracking technology to measure and analyze eye movements in real time while reading. Beyond simply scoring reading performance, it measures fixation count, fixation duration, regression count, binocular coordination, reading speed, and blink patterns to provide objective data on an individual’s reading habits and cognitive strengths and weaknesses.

Based on this data, reading level is compared against age-group norms, helping to accurately diagnose the underlying causes of reading difficulties. It also enables the design of an optimized, personalized training program and the development of effective reading strategies.

Understanding Cognitive Processes Through Eye Movement Analysis

Reading is not merely the act of scanning text with the eyes — it is an activity in which complex cognitive processes occur simultaneously. As we read, our eyes move in consistent patterns, and these eye movements directly reflect the brain’s activity in comprehending and processing text.

The Relationship Between Eye Movements and Cognitive Processing

When reading, eye movements fall into two main categories:

Fixation: The moment the eye pauses and focuses on a word. During this brief interval, the brain recognizes the text and extracts meaning. When reading speed is slow or comprehension is poor, fixation duration increases and fixation count rises.

Saccade: The rapid movement of the eye from one word to the next. Unlike fixations, saccades do not involve recognition of text meaning. When reading difficulties are present, saccades may be irregular in size, and regressive saccades — backward movements — occur more frequently.

By analyzing eye movement patterns — fixation duration, saccade count, and regression frequency — it is possible to identify not only surface-level reading problems (speed, accuracy) but also the underlying cognitive causes (attention, working memory, visual-perceptual processing).

item.title: Gymtop Sensory Integration
item.description:
Gymtop Sensory Integration Training

Integrative training for balance, coordination, and sensory processing, improving body regulation in children with sensory processing difficulties.

Training Principles

  4. Builds the foundation for self-regulation and attention

Applications

  • Co-occurring ADHD and sensory processing issues

item.title: Intelligence Assessment
item.description:
What is an Intelligence Assessment?

An intelligence assessment is not simply a test to confirm an IQ number. It analyzes a detailed cognitive profile — including verbal comprehension, visuospatial processing, fluid reasoning, working memory, and processing speed — to objectively identify an individual’s cognitive strengths and vulnerabilities.

Assessment Instruments

Children & Adolescents

K-WISC-V (Ages 6 years to 16 years 11 months)

  • Verbal Comprehension Index: vocabulary, verbal reasoning ability
  • Visual Spatial Index: visual information processing, spatial construction ability
  • Fluid Reasoning Index: logical thinking, problem-solving ability
  • Working Memory Index: ability to retain and manipulate information
  • Processing Speed Index: cognitive processing speed and accuracy

Adults

K-WAIS-IV (Ages 16 to 69)

  • Verbal Comprehension Index: vocabulary, general knowledge, comprehension
  • Perceptual Reasoning Index: visual problem-solving, spatial processing
  • Working Memory Index: attention, short-term memory, mental manipulation
  • Processing Speed Index: visual-motor coordination, processing speed

Assessment Overview

  • Duration: 60–90 minutes
  • Target: Children aged 6 and above through adults
  • Method: 1:1 individual assessment with a specialist
  • Report: Comprehensive interpretive report and feedback consultation within 1–2 weeks after completion

Recommended For

  • When you want to understand the cognitive causes behind academic underperformance
  • When cognitive decline or burnout in adults is a concern
  • When a baseline cognitive profile is needed before neurofeedback or cognitive training

item.title: Neurofeedback
item.description:
Neurofeedback Equipment

Real-time brainwave measurement via scalp electrodes provides audiovisual feedback when target frequency bands are achieved, strengthening the brain’s self-regulation capacity.

How It Works

  1. Scalp electrodes record real-time EEG signals
  2. Activation of target frequency bands (e.g., SMR, alpha, theta) is analyzed in real time
  3. Positive feedback (visual/auditory) is provided when the target is achieved
  4. Repeated training improves the brain’s self-regulatory ability

Applications

  • ADHD and reduced attention
  • Anxiety and hyperarousal regulation
  • Sleep quality improvement
  • Peak Performance training

item.title: QEEG Brain Function Assessment
item.description:
Purpose of the Brain Function Assessment

Neurofeedback training is a scientifically grounded method that enhances the brain’s self-regulation capacity through its electrical activity. A preliminary brain function assessment is conducted to objectively understand the brain’s current functional state. This allows us to identify areas requiring training and to develop a personalized training plan aligned with the individual’s goals — whether focus, emotional regulation, sleep, stress, or other concerns.

Why a Brain Function Assessment Is Needed

Brainwaves are closely related to psychological and physical states. Attention deficits, hyperactivity, anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, chronic stress, and emotional dysregulation can each be associated with patterns of over- or under-activation in specific brain regions. By directly measuring brainwave patterns, we design training grounded in neurological evidence.

How the Assessment Is Conducted

The EEG assessment examines the function of each brain region according to the 10–20 international system. Sensors are attached to the scalp to measure the brain’s electrical activity in a resting state. The assessment typically includes recordings with eyes closed (resting EEG) and eyes open (alert EEG). There is no pain or stimulation during the assessment, and children can take it comfortably.

item.title: tVNS (Transcutaneous Vagus Nerve Stimulation)
item.description:
tVNS — Transcutaneous Vagus Nerve Stimulation

Micro-current delivered to the skin around the ear (auricular region) stimulates the vagus nerve and activates the parasympathetic nervous system.

How It Works

  1. Small electrodes attached to the auricular region of the ear
  2. Gentle electrical stimulation travels via the auricular branch of the vagus nerve to the brainstem
  3. Activates parasympathetic nervous system; modulates norepinephrine and acetylcholine
  4. Promotes relaxation and recovery; enhances neuroplasticity

Applications

  • Hyperarousal and chronic stress
  • Attention and focus enhancement
  • Pre-session preparation for neurofeedback
  • Cases requiring parasympathetic activation

item.title: Frequently Asked Questions
item.description:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. What happens during the first visit? The first visit begins with an initial consultation and cognitive profiling session. Over approximately 2.5 to 3 hours, you will complete a personalized battery of assessments to identify your current state and goals, after which a tailored training plan is designed together. Regular training sessions follow from there.

Q. How many sessions are needed? It depends on individual goals and initial assessment results, but a minimum of 20–40 sessions is generally recommended. Changes in brain and autonomic nervous system function occur gradually through repeated training, and progress is monitored through periodic assessments.

Q. When do the effects become noticeable? Individual results vary, but many people begin to notice improvements in focus, sleep quality, and emotional regulation around sessions 10–15. Brain training works like muscle training — consistent repetition is key.

Q. Can children participate? Yes, absolutely. Training is available for children aged 5 and above, with protocols adapted to each child’s age and developmental level. A parent or guardian consultation and initial assessment are conducted before training begins to confirm suitability.

Q. Can adults participate? Yes, adults are welcome. We offer personalized training for a wide range of adult concerns, including burnout, sleep difficulties, social anxiety, reduced concentration, and stress regulation.

Q. Can training be combined with medication? Yes, it can. Neurofeedback and cognitive training are non-invasive and are not intended to replace medication, but rather to complement it. We recommend consulting with your physician before beginning training.

Q. Are there any side effects? Neurofeedback, biofeedback, and cognitive training are non-invasive and drug-free, making them generally safe. A small number of individuals may experience temporary fatigue or mild headache during the first few sessions, which typically resolves within 1–2 days. tVNS uses very low current levels and is virtually painless. Please inform us in advance if you have epilepsy, a cardiac pacemaker, or any other specific medical condition.
